newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German builders, employers prepare for talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German builders, employers prepare for talks.

text.p: Employers and unions in Germany's troubled construction industry continued their war of words on Tuesday as both sides sought to establish parameters for a fresh round of wage talks.

Crucial differences between the two sides remain, but both sides said they were prepared to sit around a table to enter talks aimed at pulling the industry back from the brink of its first wide-scale strike since 1950.

Employers kicked off the horse-trading earlier in the day when they offered the IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt (IG Bau) building union a new round of wage talks and said that the negotiations could take place later this week.
The response from the wages commission of IG Bau was positive, when a spokesman responded saying that the union was prepared to take part in fresh pay talks.
While employers and unions agree on the need for talks, crucial differences between the two sides remain.
IG Bau insisted that the basis for discussions had to be the full payment of sick pay from day one of illness.

IG Bau also said that it would not consider a new pay deal brokered by the arbitrator, the Christian Democrat politician Heiner Geissler, and that Geissler could attend the talks only as a moderator, not as an arbitrator.

However, Wilhelm Kuechler, vice-president of the employers' group HDB, said that the talks would have to take place without IG Bau making the full payment of sick pay benefits one of the pre-conditions.
And employers went on to say that Geissler should come up with new proposals on the issue of sick-pay.

Cutting back on the full payment of sick pay benefits to German workers has been at the centre of employer/union disputes of late and cuts in sick pay benefits was the chief reason why IG Bau's wages commission on Monday urged union leaders to reject an arbitration-brokered pay deal.

IG Bau was demanding that its members receive 100 percent of sick pay benefits, while the pay-deal brokered by the arbitrator allowed for a payment of 80 percent of sick pay benefits for the first three weeks of illness.
Klaus Wiesehugel, head of IG Bau, said on Monday that the union was prepared to compensate for the full payment of 100 percent of sick pay costs, saying it was "a matter of principles."
Meanwhile in Bonn, Peter Huber, vice-president of the ZDB building employers union, said there was no way it could accept the conditions set out by the union with no ifs or buts.
If a deal is not approved by May 21, IG Bau can lawfully call for industrial action.

German construction minister Klaus Toepfer, speaking on German radio, called for a conciliation between the sides and said that an industrial dispute would only cause further damage in an already weakened industry.

Analysts believe that any strike is likely to be limited since neither side can afford a prolonged dispute in a sector suffering from mass employment, with about 400,000 of its 1.3 million workers out of a job.
